verses.text: Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength.
Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name; worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness.
The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders; the LORD is heard over many waters.
The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is majestic.
The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars; the LORD shatters the cedars of Lebanon.
He makes Lebanon skip like a calf, and Sirion like a young wild ox.
The voice of the LORD strikes with flames of fire.
The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness; the LORD shakes the Wilderness of Kadesh.
The voice of the LORD twists the oaks and strips the forests bare. And in His temple all cry, "Glory!"
The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD is enthroned as King forever.
The LORD gives His people strength; the LORD blesses His people with peace.

context.author: The title says “of David” (Hebrew le-David), which can mean by David, for David or about David. Seventy-three psalms carry his name; tradition and the New Testament take many of them as his.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.mapLabel: THE STORM FROM LEBANON TO THE WILDERNESS
context.setting: The psalm calls the “heavenly beings” to give the LORD glory (vv.1-2), then follows a thunderstorm across the land. Seven times it says “the voice of the LORD.” The storm rolls in over the Mediterranean, “over many waters” (v.3), crashes into the mountains of the north, where “the LORD shatters the cedars of Lebanon” and makes Lebanon and Sirion skip like young animals (vv.5-6), flashes with lightning (v.7), and sweeps south to shake “the Wilderness of Kadesh” (v.8). Meanwhile, “in His temple all cry, Glory!” (v.9). “The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD is enthroned as King forever” (v.10), and He gives His people strength and peace (v.11).
context.custom: The Canaanites credited storms to Baal, the storm god, whose voice was the thunder; texts from Ugarit (about 1300 BC) use language close to this psalm. Psalm 29 gives that glory to the LORD alone. Sirion was the Sidonian name for Mount Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9). Cedars of Lebanon were the tallest, strongest trees known, used for palaces and temples.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 30 thanks God for healing: “Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning.”
context.timelineBible: The word for “flood” in v.10, mabbul, is used elsewhere only for Noah’s flood in Genesis 6-11. When God spoke from heaven to Jesus, some in the crowd said it had thundered (John 12:28-29). In Revelation, seven thunders speak (Revelation 10:3-4).

translation.meaning: Voice, sound, thunder. Used seven times in the psalm.
Cedar, the great tree of Lebanon.
The flood, the great deluge; used only of Noah’s flood and here.

gospelParallels.note: The crowd said it had thundered.
Even the winds and the sea obey Him.

otBackground.note: The LORD was not in the wind or the earthquake.

overview.summary: A thunderstorm sweeps from the sea over Lebanon to the southern wilderness, and every crash is the voice of the LORD, who reigns over the flood and gives His people peace.
overview.settingLine: A storm from the sea over the mountains.

history.t: Its texts share the psalm’s storm language.

customs.t: The voice of the LORD seven times.

archaeology.t: Baal myths from Ras Shamra in Syria, about 1300 BC.
A carved Baal with a thunderbolt club, from Ugarit, now in the Louvre.

overview.discussion: The storm that terrifies the land is God’s voice, and it ends in “peace” (v.11). How does God’s power become comfort for His people?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-100 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David
overview.genre: Hymn: the LORD of the storm
